title: How To Avoid Dangerous Student Behavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the retreat from firm consequences toward purely restorative discipline has directly caused a rise in dangerous student behavior, since students who can fight, threaten, or throw chairs without suspension inevitably repeat that behavior. Rather than dwelling on administrative policy, the piece focuses on nine SCM-aligned practices a teacher can control that virtually eliminate dangerous behavior on their own watch: clarity of boundaries, small-scale accountability, genuine rapport, calmness, order, purpose-driven lessons, close supervision, day-to-day consistency, and consistent experiences of success. His central claim is that following through on minor, everyday accountability prevents the escalation to major, dangerous incidents, and that these strategies require full commitment rather than partial adoption to be reliably protective.
points: The shift toward purely restorative discipline without firm consequences is directly linked to a rise in dangerous student behavior like fighting and threats.
Consistently following through on small, everyday accountability is framed as what prevents escalation to major, dangerous behavioral incidents.
Precise, detailed teaching of nonnegotiable boundaries ahead of time is described as freeing students to relax, since they know the teacher will protect them.
The nine protective practices require full commitment rather than partial adoption; 'dabbling' in the approach is explicitly said not to be enough.
quotes: The jettisoning of firm consequences in favor of a purely restorative approach has caused more dangerous behavior among students.
Nowadays, a student can fight, bully, torment, throw chairs, and threaten a teacher without being suspended. The result, of course, is that they do it again and again and again.
Your precise and detailed teaching of your nonnegotiable boundaries ahead of time free students to relax in knowing that you will protect them.
Following through on the little things as defined by your classroom management plan keep the big things from ever happening.
But it takes not just dabbling in SCM, but a complete embrace.
